title: Growing chard microgreens
subtitle: Colourful cotyledons with a mild earthy flavour, cut in 10 to 14 days
excerpt: Chard microgreens produce cotyledons in a range of stem colours depending on the variety: red, yellow, orange, and white stems with green or reddish seed leaves. The flavour is milder than beetroot microgreens and suits salads and grain bowls. Cycle is 10 to 14 days.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Chard microgreens are a year-round indoor tray crop with a 10 to 14 day cycle. Sow on a pre-dampened seed compost tray, blackout for three to four days, then grow in light until the cotyledons are 5 to 8 cm tall. Rainbow chard varieties produce cotyledons with red, yellow, orange, or white stems; the visual variety makes chard microgreens useful as a colourful garnish and salad ingredient.

Like beetroot, chard seed is a corky multi-germ cluster rather than a true single seed. Germination is slightly more reliable than beetroot and the clusters separate more easily when rubbed between the palms before sowing.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill in spring and summer. A grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray at 14 to 16 hours per day is recommended in winter. Chard microgreens in low light produce pale, elongated cotyledons without the vivid stem colouring.
Temperature: 16 to 22°C. Chard is one of the more cold-tolerant microgreen crops and will germinate adequately at 14°C, though the cycle extends to 14 to 16 days at the lower end.

Day 0: sow. Fill the tray with pre-dampened seed compost to within 1 cm of the rim. Rub the chard seed clusters lightly between your palms before sowing to partially break them apart. Scatter at 20 to 25 g per 25 cm tray. Press gently into contact with the medium.
Days 1 to 4: blackout. Cover with a second tray, lightly weighted. Chard germinates in three to four days; remove the cover when the majority of shoots are upright at 2 to 3 cm.
Day 5 onward: light. Stem colours develop within 24 to 48 hours of moving to a bright position.
daily: set the growing tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water. Remove excess after 30 minutes.
Days 10 to 14: cut. When cotyledons are fully open and 5 to 8 cm tall, cut 1 cm above the medium surface. Rinse and use fresh or refrigerate for up to two days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on chard microgreen trays.

items.cause: Chard seed clusters not separated before sowing.
items.fix: Rub the clusters between your palms more firmly before sowing. Each cluster can be broken into smaller pieces; this distributes the seedlings more evenly across the tray.

items.symptom: Pale stems — no colour development after moving to light
items.fix: Increase light intensity or duration. Note that white-stemmed chard (for example Fordhook Giant) will always produce pale stems; the colour you see is the variety's natural characteristic.

items.cause: Cold room or seed buried too deep.
items.fix: Warm the room above 16°C. Ensure seed is pressed into contact with the medium surface rather than buried.

content.text: Use untreated chard seed. Rainbow chard mixtures (sold under various names: 'Rainbow', 'Five Colour Silverbeet', 'Bright Lights') produce the most visually varied cotyledons. For a consistent colour rather than a mix, use a single-colour variety. Microgreen seed suppliers stock chard seed in pack sizes suited to tray growing.
risk is moderate. Bottom-water only and ensure adequate airflow.
